content: Naproxen sodium is a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) that is used to relieve pain, reduce inflammation, and manage various conditions such as ankylosing spondylitis, bursitis, acute gout, osteoarthritis, primary dysmenorrhea, rheumatoid arthritis, and tendinitis. It is available in different formulations, including immediate-release and controlled-release tablets, as well as over-the-counter (OTC) options. Adult Dosage Guidelines: 1. Ankylosing Spondylitis: Immediate-release: 275 mg or 550 mg twice daily (morning and evening). Dosage adjustments may be made based on clinical response. Long-term use may require lower doses, but up to 1650 mg/day can be used for 6 months in patients tolerating lower doses. Controlled-release: 750 mg to 1000 mg once daily. If the initial response is inadequate, the dose may be increased to 1500 mg once daily for a limited time. The smallest effective dose should be used. 2. Bursitis: Immediate-release: 550 mg initially, followed by 550 mg every 12 hours or 275 mg every 6–8 hours as needed. The maximum daily dose is 1375 mg on the first day and 1100 mg/day thereafter. Controlled-release: 1000 mg once daily, with the option to increase to 1500 mg once daily for a limited time if pain relief is insufficient. Once pain is controlled, the dose should not exceed 1000 mg daily. 3. Acute Gout: Immediate-release: 825 mg initially, followed by 275 mg every 8 hours until symptoms subside. Controlled-release: 1000–1500 mg on the first day, followed by 1000 mg once daily until the attack resolves. 4. Osteoarthritis: Immediate-release: 275 mg or 550 mg twice daily. Dosage adjustments may be made based on clinical response. Long-term use may require lower doses, but up to 1650 mg/day can be used for 6 months in patients tolerating lower doses. Controlled-release: 750 mg to 1000 mg once daily. If the initial response is inadequate, the dose may be increased to 1500 mg once daily for a limited time. The smallest effective dose should be used. 5. Pain (Mild to Moderate), Acute Tendonitis, and Bursitis: Immediate-release: 550 mg initially, followed by 550 mg every 12 hours or 275 mg every 6–8 hours as needed. The maximum daily dose is 1375 mg on the first day and 1100 mg/day thereafter. Controlled-release: 1000 mg once daily, with the option to increase to 1500 mg once daily for a limited time if pain relief is insufficient. Once pain is controlled, the dose should not exceed 1000 mg daily. OTC: 220–440 mg initially, followed by 220 mg every 8–12 hours as needed. Do not exceed 440 mg in any 8–12 hour period or 660 mg in 24 hours. Use for no longer than 10 days unless directed by a physician. 6. Primary Dysmenorrhea: Immediate-release: 550 mg initially, followed by 550 mg every 12 hours or 275 mg every 6–8 hours as needed. The maximum daily dose is 1375 mg on the first day and 1100 mg/day thereafter. Controlled-release: 1000 mg once daily, with the option to increase to 1500 mg once daily for a limited time if pain relief is insufficient. Once pain is controlled, the dose should not exceed 1000 mg daily. OTC: 220–440 mg initially, followed by 220 mg every 8–12 hours as needed. Do not exceed 440 mg in any 8–12 hour period or 660 mg in 24 hours. Use for no longer than 10 days unless directed by a physician. 7. Rheumatoid Arthritis: Immediate-release: 275 mg or 550 mg twice daily. Dosage adjustments may be made based on clinical response. Long-term use may require lower doses, but up to 1650 mg/day can be used for 6 months in patients tolerating lower doses. Controlled-release: 750 mg to 1000 mg once daily. If the initial response is inadequate, the dose may be increased to 1500 mg once daily for a limited time. The smallest effective dose should be used. 8. Tendinitis: Immediate-release: 550 mg initially, followed by 550 mg every 12 hours or 275 mg every 6–8 hours as needed. The maximum daily dose is 1375 mg on the first day and 1100 mg/day thereafter. Controlled-release: 1000 mg once daily, with the option to increase to 1500 mg once daily for a limited time if pain relief is insufficient. Once pain is controlled, the dose should not exceed 1000 mg daily. Pediatric Dosage Guidelines: 1. Fever (12 years and older): OTC: 220–440 mg initially, followed by 220 mg every 8–12 hours as needed. Do not exceed 440 mg in any 8–12 hour period or 660 mg in 24 hours. Use for no longer than 10 days unless directed by a physician. 2. Pain (12 years and older): OTC: 220–440 mg initially, followed by 220 mg every 8–12 hours as needed. Do not exceed 440 mg in any 8–12 hour period or 660 mg in 24 hours. Use for no longer than 10 days unless directed by a physician. 3. Primary Dysmenorrhea (12 years and older): OTC: 220–440 mg initially, followed by 220 mg every 8–12 hours as needed. Do not exceed 440 mg in any 8–12 hour period or 660 mg in 24 hours. Use for no longer than 10 days unless directed by a physician. 4. Juvenile Rheumatoid Arthritis (2 years and older): The recommended total daily dose is approximately 10 mg/kg, divided into two doses (5 mg/kg twice daily). Naproxen suspension is preferred for pediatric patients to allow for flexible dosing. Warnings and Precautions: 1. Allergic Reactions: Naproxen sodium may cause severe allergic reactions, particularly in individuals allergic to aspirin. Symptoms include hives, facial swelling, wheezing, shock, skin reddening, rash, and blisters. Discontinue use and seek medical attention immediately if an allergic reaction occurs. 2. Stomach Bleeding Risk: This medication contains an NSAID, which may increase the risk of severe stomach bleeding, especially in individuals aged 60 or older, those with a history of stomach ulcers or bleeding, those taking anticoagulants or steroids, those consuming three or more alcoholic drinks daily, or those taking the medication for longer than directed. 3. Contraindications: Do not use naproxen sodium if you have had an allergic reaction to any pain reliever/fever reducer or immediately before or after heart surgery. 4. Pregnancy and Breastfeeding: Avoid use during the last three months of pregnancy unless specifically directed by a physician, as it may cause complications for the unborn child or during delivery. 5. Heart and Stroke Risk: Prolonged use or exceeding the recommended dose may increase the risk of heart attack or stroke. Adverse Reactions: Common side effects include edema, ecchymosis, pruritus, rash, abdominal pain, constipation, heartburn, nausea, dizziness, headache, somnolence, ototoxicity, tinnitus, and dyspnea. Administration and Monitoring: Take with food or milk to minimize stomach upset. Use the smallest effective dose for the shortest duration necessary to achieve therapeutic effects. Overdose: In case of overdose, seek immediate medical attention or contact a Poison Control Center. Patient Counseling: Do not exceed the recommended dose. Drink a full glass of water with each dose. Avoid alcohol while taking this medication unless advised otherwise by a healthcare provider.
